description: We are Team Neuru Volex, four engineering students from Pakistan: Shahzaman Jatoi, Alisha, Aisha and Zara. Our team is complete and not looking for new members. We’re preparing early for NASA Space Apps 2026 to build a practical solution using NASA data.
summary:
Real space missions don't fail because the rocket wasn't big enough they fail because adding one extra sensor drains the battery during an orbital eclipse, or overflows onboard memory before the spacecraft ever reaches a ground station.

MissionCraft turns those high-stakes aerospace trade-offs into a playable 3D systems-engineering simulation.

Built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, MissionCraft puts you in the seat of a NASA Mission Systems Engineer. Instead of building with unlimited resources, every component you bolt onto your spacecraft triggers real physical consequences across six coupled constraints: mass, power, budget, onboard data, communications downlink, and mission timeline. Upgrade your spectrometer for higher science returns, and you immediately feel the squeeze on your solar arrays, rocket payload limit, and ground-station bandwidth.

Once your spacecraft passes launch-vehicle compatibility checks, you launch into an interactive 3D orbital simulation navigating Earth's shadow on battery reserves and racing to downlink science packets during narrow communication passes. If your mission fails, you don't just get a "Game Over" screen; you get a diagnostic engineering post-mortem explaining the exact physics that broke your spacecraft, challenging you to iterate like a real mission architect.
details:
MissionCraft is a space mission design game where you build a mission, fly it, and learn from the result.

What it does: Pick a destination (Low Earth Orbit, GEO, the Moon or Mars), choose a rocket, and design your spacecraft, from engine and antenna to instruments, power and battery. A live panel checks delta-v, mass, power, battery, communications and cost, and gives a mission score out of 100. Then you fly it in a simulation with live telemetry and replay. In an eclipse, you decide: maintain full load or conserve power. A debrief explains the outcome, and success unlocks the next destination, up to Mars.

Impact: Students rarely get to design a whole mission, so the trade-offs stay abstract. MissionCraft makes them playable. It needs no expertise and runs in any browser.

Built with: React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Three.js (React Three Fiber), Tailwind CSS and Framer Motion, deployed on Vercel. The engineering and simulation engine is our own code.

Creative edge: It covers the full cycle of design, launch, fly and debrief. Operational decisions affect the outcome, and the instruments are modeled on NASA's LRO (LROC, LOLA, Diviner).

NASA resources: LRO, Mission Design Lab, Concept Maturity Levels, GMAT and CubeSat resources.

What we considered: accessibility, honest trade-offs with no single perfect design, and learning over scoring. It is an educational prototype, not a flight-planning tool.
dataRefs: NASA Ames mission-design and concept-maturity resources
